added_claim_errors: 'United's travel credits are typically valid for one year from issuance': an unverified claim about United's policy that also conflicts with DOT's rule that a credit offered in lieu of a refund must stay valid for at least 5 years
Calls the one-year ask 'reasonable and standard': wrong, because the legal minimum is 5 years
'Weather affects what the airline owes you in compensation': misleading, because US law requires no cash compensation for a cancellation whatever the cause
Says a credit is 'typically good for about a year' and that 'at least a year' is 'roughly the standard': wrong, because a credit offered in lieu of a refund must stay valid for at least 5 years

'A DOT complaint usually unblocks it': a soft claim with no support (minor). The quoted rule wording 'applies irrespective of the reason for a cancellation' checks out: I opened the govinfo link and found it in 89 FR 32760, at page 32770

reasons: B corrects the agent's false claim in its first line and tells the person not to take the credit. It drafts a refund request for $412 to the original payment method, citing 14 CFR part 260 and the 7-business-day deadline, and backs this with a real Federal Register link and a quote that checks out. A writes the message that accepts the credit, which is exactly what the key deducts for. It says the person is owed a refund only in a footnote after the draft, and it calls a one-year credit 'standard'. Both answers miss the 5-year minimum for credits, and B leaves out the 20-day deadline for other payment forms. Even so, B gets the person their $412 and A gives it away.
